sets.hill: Night hilltop observing field, Jump treatment. far: SpaceBackdrop #080614 with dense stars and a faint Milky Way band; mid: two layered dark ridge silhouettes with a pale rim line; near: GroundPlane of dry grass with pale rim and two dark outlined rocks. setp.rate 0..1 = meteor density: thin cream/gold streaks with a bloom head, 40-140 px long, all radiating from a radiant point near (0.5, 0.1), count round(rate*55) alive at once, each on its own phase so nothing visibly repeats; at rate 0 none, at 0.05 one rare streak. setp.tint 'cold' (default) | 'dawn' (warm orange horizon glow) | 'red'. setp.sickle 1 draws the backwards-question-mark Leo Sickle in bright dots at the radiant.
sets.summit: Mountain observatory (Kitt Peak / Table Mountain style): the hill set plus a pale-rimmed dome silhouette with an open slit on the left, a telescope tube pointing up through it, a small lit window with warm Glow, a dirt access road in the mid ground. setp.rate as hill. setp.tint cold|dawn.
sets.town1833: 1833 New England night. far: stars with meteors by setp.rate (same streak rule as hill); mid: row of dark rooftops with chimneys and a church spire, three warm lit windows (Glow); near: cobbled street GroundPlane, one lantern post with warm bloom. setp.rate 0..1.
sets.space: Deep-space diagram scene: SpaceBackdrop with slow rays. setp.view: 'comet' = small dark rock with a bright coma and two tails (white-blue ion tail straight, pale yellow dust tail curved) travelling right with a Sun glow far left; 'trail' = a wide translucent dotted dust band curving across the frame with Earth (small blue-green disc, pale rim) crossing it at the centre; 'orbits' = Sun glow centre, thin dashed cream ellipses for Earth's orbit and the comet's long oval orbit, Jupiter as a gold disc on a wider ring; 'far' = tiny Sun, a huge dark gap, the comet as a pin-prick far out past a Saturn ring. setp.t 0..1 animates the main body along its path.
sets.atmos: Edge of Earth's atmosphere seen from the side: curved planet limb along the bottom (deep blue disc, pale rim), a thin cyan atmosphere glow band above it, stars above. setp.rate meteors enter from the upper right as bright streaks that flare and vanish at the glow band, with a small bloom flash. setp.speed 0..1 streak length.
sets.city: Night Central Park, 1966. far: skyline silhouettes with many warm lit windows; mid: park lawn GroundPlane with hundreds of tiny warm dots (lanterns/flashlights, no figures) and a few bare tree silhouettes; sky: setp.clouds 0..1 = thick flat dark-grey outlined cloud banks sliding over the stars (0 clear, 1 total overcast).
sets.garden: Present-day back garden before dawn, 2026. far: deep sky fading to a thin dawn-orange horizon, stars, Leo's Sickle, Mars (small red disc) and Jupiter (small gold disc) side by side with bloom; mid: dark fence line and a house roof edge; near: frosty GroundPlane with pale rim, a patio chair. setp.rate 0..0.1 rare streaks. setp.frost 1 adds sparkle dots on the ground.
sets.void: Plain deep-navy SpaceBackdrop stage with slow light rays and almost no stars, for big numbers, bars and diagrams. setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red' tints the rays.

props.counter: Big flat panel, 4 px dark outline, dark #1E1B2E face, cream flip digits in FONTS.title with thousands separators, label in FONTS.ui underneath. pp.from and pp.to: the number counts up from->to across the shot (ease-out); pp.label text; pp.color gold|red|cyan.
props.clock: Round analogue clock face, cream disc, 4 px dark outline, ticks, one hand. pp.from..pp.to in minutes: the hand sweeps; pp.glow true adds a gold bloom.
props.umbrella: Big flat umbrella, hood-teal #2FB7A6 panels with dark outline, mustard handle; tiny gold sparks bounce off the canopy when pp.hit is true. Held above Pip as an overlay (pip.held).
props.telescope: Small tripod telescope: dark tube, mustard ring, three outlined legs, soft rim light.
props.thermos: Mustard thermos flask with a dark cap and a little steam curl (Glow).
props.blanket: Overlay for PipLocal: checked mustard-and-dark blanket draped over Pip's shoulders, sits below the head, never covers the face.
props.clipboard: Flat clipboard with cream sheet; pp.marks = number of tally strokes drawn on in sequence; dark outline.
props.bar: Horizontal progress bar with 4 px outline, filled with pp.color (gold|red|cyan) to pp.frac of its width over the shot; pp.label above in FONTS.ui.
props.chair: Fold-out lawn chair, dark frame, teal canvas, outlined, a soft rim.
props.sign: Hand-painted sign on a post, cream board, dark outline, pp.text in FONTS.hand (max 12 chars).
props.earth: Small Earth disc, blue-green with simple outlined continents, pale rim, subtle atmosphere glow. pp.tilt degrees.
props.dust: Cloud of small cream dots of dust drifting slowly with a faint bloom; pp.density 0..1.
props.stopwatch: Round outlined stopwatch, cream face, red button on top; pp.from..pp.to seconds: hand sweeps and the digits count.
props.headlamp: Overlay for PipLocal: tiny headlamp strap on the hood with a warm beam cone (Glow, 0.25 opacity) pointing up-right.
props.jupiter: Gold-and-cream banded Jupiter disc with dark outline, pale rim, bloom; pp.s scale; subtle band drift.
props.calendar: Wall calendar card, cream page, 4 px dark outline, big year in FONTS.title from pp.year; page flips once with a settle when p passes 0.3 if pp.flip.

actions.lookup: Pip tilts head back (headTilt up), arms hang loose, small sway; eyes lift at p 0.2.
actions.duck: Pip drops into a crouch with both arms raised over the head at p 0.15 and holds with a small tremble.
actions.spin: Pip turns one slow full rotation (yaw/spin) across the shot while looking up.
actions.flinch: A quick squash and lean away at p 0.2 with arms up, then settles back by p 0.7.
actions.pointup: Pip's arm swings up to point at the sky at p 0.2 with a small overshoot.

chapters.title: THE NIGHT NEW YORK LOOKED UP

film.vo: Forty shooting stars.
Every. Single. Second.
For a whole hour.
One hundred forty-four thousand streaks of fire.
That is what thirteen people saw, from one mountain in Arizona.
In nineteen sixty-six.
And they ducked.
film.dir: flat, then a laugh in the voice

film.vo: This week, those same meteors are back.
You will be lucky to see fifteen an hour.
So what if you had been standing there, in sixty-six?
What if the sky just let go?
Here are the rules.
You stand on a dark hill, far from any city.
The sky is perfectly clear.
The Moon is gone.
You have exactly one hour.
And you get a thermos of something hot.
Your only job is to keep your eyes open.
Because blinking, tonight, means missing something.
And here is the catch.
This only happens when the Earth drives through something.
And nobody can book it in advance.
Minute one. A single streak crosses the sky.
Then another.
Then three at once.
You stop counting, because you cannot keep up.
One astronomer called it a rain of meteors.
That turned into a hail of meteors.
And then a storm.
Too many to count, by ten to four in the morning.
He said they instinctively shielded their faces.
From pieces of dust. High above.
Each one slams into the air at forty-five miles a second.
That is seventy-two kilometres every second.
Because the Leonids come at us head-on.
Earth goes one way. The dust goes the other.
Nothing on Earth moves that fast.
Bright streaks. Long glowing trails.
Some leave long-lasting trails behind them.
And you are standing under all of it, with a flask.
Hang on. How many is that, really?
Forty a second is two thousand four hundred a minute.
film.dir: steady, counting; stress 'two thousand four hundred'

film.vo: Keep that up for an hour.
And you reach one hundred forty-four thousand.
That was the peak, as seen from Kitt Peak, Arizona.
Thirteen amateur astronomers counted it.
With their eyes. And clickers. And coffee.
Now compare it with a normal year.
Fifteen an hour, in a really good sky.
So the storm outran a normal year by a lot.
That is nine thousand six hundred times more.
One storm hour equals four hundred days of this year's best sky.
A year and a bit of waiting, squeezed into sixty minutes.
By the numbers, you could not blink.
You would be seeing a meteor in every blink of the eye.
So where does all this stuff come from?
film.dir: question that opens the next chapter

film.vo: A comet. Its name is Tempel-Tuttle.
It loops around the Sun once every thirty-three years.
Thirty-three and a third, to be fair.
Each time it swings close to the Sun, it sheds.
Dust. Grit. Crumbs of ice.
Like a river of rubble left behind it.
The trail stays in space for centuries.
And once a year, the Earth drives straight through the edge of it.
Thin edge: a trickle of meteors.
But a direct hit on a fresh clump?
That is when the sky opens.
A storm needs fresh debris, thrown out within the last few centuries.
The comet last passed the Sun in nineteen ninety-eight.
The sky lit up in ninety-nine, oh-one, and oh-two.
A few thousand an hour, at best.
Then the dust ran thin, year after year.
And back in eighteen thirty-three, it did the same thing.
Tens of thousands an hour, they say.
It must have looked like the sky was falling.
Just comet dust, hitting the air at tremendous speed.
Which brings us back to nineteen sixty-six.
Scientists had done their sums.
The comet was in the same place as in eighteen thirty-three.
So a big shower might be coming.
New York planned a meteor party.
Midnight. Central Park. The Great Lawn.
Ten thousand people turned up.
And the sky was completely clouded over.
Ten thousand people looked up and saw... grey.
Meanwhile, out west, skies were clear.
In Texas, one person saw them fall like a gigantic umbrella.
Right out of the head of Leo, the Lion.
You, with a real umbrella, would still get wet.
So you'd better pray for clear skies.
Because the whole show depends on one thing.
So, here is the catch for this year.
Right now, Tempel-Tuttle is past Saturn.
About one billion seven hundred ninety million kilometres from the Sun.
It is slowly crawling back toward the Sun.
But the part of the trail Earth crosses this week?
Almost empty.
Just a few scattered crumbs, loose for a thousand years or two.
So no storm. Not this week.
Experts expect long stretches of nothing at all.
Which makes the next question the real one.
So what will you actually see?
The Leonids peak on the seventeenth and eighteenth of November.
The IMO puts the peak at quarter to midnight UTC, the seventeenth.
NASA says: look before dawn, after the Moon sets.
Leo climbs higher after midnight.
Up to fifteen an hour, if everything goes right.
Most people will see fewer.
But look at who is next to them.
On the fifteenth and sixteenth, Mars and Jupiter sit side by side.
Only one point two degrees apart.
That is about two Moons wide.
Find a dark spot, and give your eyes half an hour.
Bring a blanket. A flask. A friend.
And look at as much of the sky as you can.
One streak is plenty. It is the fastest thing you will ever see.
Forty-five miles a second, remember.
So when does the sky let go again?
Not for a while, sadly.
In twenty twenty-nine, Jupiter is expected to nudge the comet off course.
After that, a repeat of the great storm is basically off the table.
Basically. Not quite.
One French expert forecast a big burst in twenty thirty-four.
Up to two thousand an hour.
That is eight years from now.
Not a storm like sixty-six, but a sky with hail in it.
So, back to that mountain in Arizona.
Forty meteors a second, and you are the one standing under them.
You would never need to ask what the sky is made of again.
film.dir: warm; a laugh at the end

film.vo: You would know it falls.
Which night would you pick: eighteen thirty-three, or sixty-six?
Tomorrow: another what if, another piece of the sky.

short.vo: Nineteen sixty-six. Thirteen people, one mountain in Arizona.
One hundred forty-four thousand meteors in an hour.
It comes from a comet. Tempel-Tuttle.
It leaves a river of dust behind it.
Once a year, Earth drives through the edge.
Hit a fresh clump, and the sky opens.
Facing us, they strike at forty-five miles a second.
Ten thousand New Yorkers came to watch it.
This week the Leonids are back.
But the dust is thin this year.
So look before dawn, after the Moon sets.
The next big burst: twenty thirty-four.
Full film on the channel. Tomorrow: another what if.

short.dir: punch; echo of the first line
